analysis.one_liner: Bans ATM operators from charging extra fees when consumers use another bank's machine.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred ATM surcharges, never got a vote: after being referred to the House Banking Committee and a subcommittee in spring 1996, it sat there until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend a 1978 consumer law, the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, to stop the company or bank that runs an ATM from charging you a fee for using their machine when your account is at a different bank. It targets the "surcharge" — the extra fee tacked on by the machine's owner — that was spreading in the mid-1990s. The bill would not stop your own bank from charging you for using a machine outside its network.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who use ATMs away from their own bank — tourists, workers getting cash near their job, anyone whose bank has few machines — would save the surcharge on every out-of-network withdrawal. The ban would apply to the fee charged by the machine's operator when the transaction runs over a national or regional network [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the operator of an ATM from imposing any fee on a consumer who uses that machine while their account is at another bank, when the transaction runs over a national or regional network
Writes the ban into the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, the federal consumer law that already governs electronic withdrawals, giving consumers a federal rule rather than a patchwork of state rules

analysis.who_pays: Banks and other ATM operators would lose the surcharge revenue they were beginning to collect from non-customers. If operators decided uncharged machines no longer paid for themselves, some ATMs — particularly in convenience stores, bars, and other remote spots — might be removed or not installed, leaving some consumers with fewer machines to choose from.

drawbacks.text: The bill bans only the fee charged by the machine's operator; your own bank could still charge you for using an out-of-network machine, so a consumer could not be sure of escaping fees entirely

Banks and independent operators argued then, as now, that surcharges pay for placing machines where they get little traffic, so a ban could mean fewer ATMs in convenience stores, rural areas, and low-income neighborhoods — a cost that would fall on the same consumers the bill protects

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit is real but modest: a few dollars saved per out-of-network withdrawal, repeated millions of times a year. The honest cost is that surcharges are one way of funding machines in places banks would not otherwise place them, and a flat ban could shrink access in those spots. A bill that capped or disclosed the fee, or that also limited the fee banks charge their own customers, might have balanced those interests better than an outright ban.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking and Financial Services Committee and then to its subcommittee on financial institutions, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, introduced the bill on March 29, 1996, and 13 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did
The bill was sent to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services on the day it was introduced
On April 4, 1996, it was referred further to the subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit
No further action appears in the record: the subcommittee and full committee never held a vote, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and ATM operators were better off because the bill died: they kept free rein to charge non-customers surcharges at the machine, a revenue stream that grew rapidly in the years after. Consumers kept paying the fee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks and ATM operators kept surcharge revenue

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote it to amend the Electronic Fund Transfer Act to bar ATM surcharges

against.name: House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never reported it out; no hearing or vote appears in its action history

against.name: Jim Leach
against.role: Chair, House Banking and Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that referred the bill to subcommittee and took no further action on it

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was an Independent and all 13 cosponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a roll-call vote, so the chamber's actual split was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from charging non-customers a surcharge at the machine, cutting off a new fee stream that was spreading in 1996. Its interest ran against consumers' interest in cheaper cash access.

industries.industry: ATM network companies (national and regional switch networks)
industries.note: The bill's ban applies only to transactions that run over a national or regional communication network, so the networks remain the required channel for out-of-bank withdrawals and the rule is enforced around them.
